glossary.gloss: Confucius himself. Legge renders the Chinese 'the Master' (Zi) for nearly every saying in the book; it always means Confucius.
Kong Qiu (551–479 BCE), the Chinese teacher whose recorded sayings make up this book. Legge uses his name (rather than 'the Master') mainly when an outsider or a ruler addresses or speaks of him.
Confucius's central ideal, ren — human-heartedness, goodness, the fully cultivated moral character of a true person. Legge also uses 'perfect virtue' and 'benevolence' for the same word.
Kind and good-hearted; another of Legge's words for ren, the warm regard for others that is the root of moral character.

The junzi — Confucius's ideal of the cultivated, principled person (literally 'son of a ruler', but for Confucius defined by character, not birth). The opposite of the 'mean man'. Legge sometimes leaves it untranslated as Chun-tsze.
The petty, small-minded person — the opposite of the superior man (junzi). 'Mean' here means low or base in character, not cruel or stingy.
Devoted respect, care, and obedience that children owe their parents — a foundational Confucian duty. 'Filial' simply means 'as a good son or daughter'.
The proper deference a younger brother owes an older one; paired with filial piety as a root of social harmony.
Li — the whole code of ritual, ceremony, manners, and correct social conduct. For Confucius, observing li shapes and expresses good character, not mere etiquette.
The Confucian doctrine that each thing and role must match its true name — a ruler must truly be a ruler, a father a father — so that words and reality align and society holds together.

Tian ming, the will or appointment of Heaven — the moral order of the cosmos that sets the bounds of a person's life and fate. Heaven for Confucius is an impersonal but morally charged power, not a personal god.
The Book of Poetry (Shijing), an ancient anthology of some three hundred songs and poems that Confucius treated as a core text for moral and cultural education.
Refined or liberal learning — letters, poetry, music, and the arts a cultivated person pursues after fulfilling basic duties. Legge also calls them 'polite arts'.
Agreeable and eager to please; obliging in manner. Confucius praises a courteous, accommodating bearing — distinct from the modern 'complacent'.
Ingratiating; flattering in a sly, calculated way to win favor. Confucius warns that an 'insinuating appearance' is rarely matched by real virtue.
Loss of calm or composure; being upset or flustered. The virtuous person feels none even when ignored.
Pertaining to the root or foundation. 'The superior man bends his attention to what is radical' means he concentrates on the fundamentals from which everything else grows.
To object or protest earnestly, pleading with someone to change course. A son may gently remonstrate with his parents.
Pay or profit from holding office; a salary or stipend. Some studied chiefly to win official emolument.
Broad-minded and impartial, embracing all without faction. 'The superior man is catholic and no partisan' — the lowercase sense, unrelated to the Catholic Church.
One who takes sides or belongs to a faction; biased toward his own group. The mean man is a partisan; the superior man is not.
Stingy; excessively sparing with money. Asked whether Kwan Chung was parsimonious, Confucius points out his extravagances.
Mean and ungenerous with money or help; stingy. Even great ability counts for little if a man is proud and niggardly.
Lacking moral restraint, especially in pleasure; unbridled. The Kwan Tsu ode expresses joy 'without being licentious'.
Rough, unpolished plainness, like that of a country person; lack of cultivation. The opposite extreme from the over-refined 'manners of a clerk'.
Superficially attractive or persuasive but hollow. The 'specious speech' of the litanist T'o sounds fine but lacks substance.
An official prayer-reader or invocator at religious ceremonies, prized for smooth, eloquent recitation.
Defiance of authority; refusal to submit to those above one. Confucius warns that extravagance and reckless daring lead to it.
Anxious care or concern. Even the sage-kings Yao and Shun felt solicitude about doing enough good for the people.
A heated dispute or quarrel. The admired friend, though wronged, entered into no altercation.
Fretful complaining or discontent; grumbling regret. Po-i and Shu-ch'i felt no repining at the hardships their virtue cost them.
Deep respect bordering on reverence. A scholar who is not grave will not call forth veneration from others.
Lack of courage; cowardice. 'To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage' — 'want' here means absence or lack.
Hard-pressed, in difficult or cramped circumstances, especially poverty. To be 'straitened and yet affecting to be at ease' is a kind of pretense.
A specialized tool or vessel good for only one use. Confucius's saying 'the accomplished scholar is not a utensil' means a cultivated person is not narrowly limited to a single function.
The ideal of the steady middle course between extremes — moderation and balance as a moral virtue. This idea became the heart of a later Confucian classic, the Doctrine of the Mean.
The state in eastern China that was Confucius's home, in present-day Shandong. Many disciples and events in the Analects belong to Lu.
A large, powerful state neighboring Lu, where Confucius once heard the Shao music and stayed for a time.
A central Chinese state where Confucius spent part of his years of travel; a ruler of Wei is discussed by the disciples.
A small state where Confucius stayed during his wanderings; from there he longed to return home to Lu.
A Chinese state descended from the earlier Shang (Yin) dynasty; Confucius cites it when discussing the records of ancient ceremonies.
A district whose duke asked Tsze-lu about Confucius. The 'Duke of Sheh' was a local lord rather than a true duke.
A place whose people had a bad reputation, so the disciples were surprised when Confucius received a boy from there.
A town whose governorship was offered to the disciple Min Tsze-ch'ien, who declined it.
A town where the disciple Tsze-yu served as governor.
A river; Min Tsze-ch'ien said he would sooner go live on its banks than accept an unwelcome official post.
A border post whose warden asked to meet Confucius and afterward spoke of him as Heaven's instrument. (Distinct from the Yi, the Book of Changes, that Confucius wished to study.)
One of Confucius's closest and most senior disciples — bold, blunt, and brave, often gently corrected by the Master for rashness. Also called by his given name Yu.

The philosopher Tsang (Zengzi), a devoted younger disciple known for daily self-examination and deep moral seriousness; later revered as a transmitter of Confucius's teaching. His personal name was Shan.
Confucius's favorite disciple, prized above all for his love of learning and quiet virtue; the Master grieved deeply at his early death. Also called Hui and Yen Hui.
A prominent disciple, eloquent, quick-witted, and successful in affairs; he often questions the Master and is sometimes told he falls short of higher virtue. His personal name was Ts'ze.
The philosopher Yu (Youzi), a disciple whose sayings on filial piety and ritual open the book. Note: 'Yu' is also the personal name of the disciple Tsze-lu, so context decides which is meant.
A younger disciple noted for learning and literary skill; the Master discusses the odes and the meaning of ceremony with him. Also called Shang.
A disciple who frequently asks Confucius about office, conduct, and how to win the people's trust.
A disciple who became governor of Wu-ch'ang and questions the Master about filial piety and good men.
A disciple known for clever talk and for being scolded by Confucius (once for sleeping in the daytime, 'rotten wood cannot be carved'). Also called Yu (Tsai Yu).
A disciple who serves as Confucius's charioteer and asks him about filial piety, wisdom, and perfect virtue.
A disciple, given name Yung, praised by Confucius as fit even to occupy the place of a prince despite humble origins.
A disciple of many practical talents, given name of Zan Yu (Yen Yu / Yen Ch'iu); Confucius judges him capable as an administrator.
The disciple Kung-hsi Hwa (Tsze-hwa), praised for his poise in receiving guests at court; also sent on a mission to Ch'i.
A disciple admired for his integrity, who politely refused the governorship of Pi rather than serve an unworthy clan.
A disciple made steward of Confucius's town who tried to decline his grain salary; the Master told him to keep it and share it.
Duke Ai of Lu, the ruler of Confucius's home state, who consults him about governing and which disciples love to learn.
Duke Ting of Lu, an earlier ruler of Confucius's home state, who asks how a prince and his ministers should treat one another.
Head of the powerful Chi (Ji) family that dominated the government of Lu; he questions Confucius about ruling and about the disciples' fitness for office.
The Ji clan, one of three noble families that had usurped much of the real power in the state of Lu; Confucius repeatedly criticizes their overreach and breaches of ritual.
A famous earlier statesman of the state of Ch'i, admired for his political success but criticized by Confucius for personal extravagance and ignorance of true propriety.
An ancient worthy who, with his brother Shu-ch'i, chose principled poverty and starvation over serving an unjust ruler; Confucius praises them as men of virtue without bitterness.
Brother of Po-i; together they are byword ancient worthies who held to their principles and bore no grudges.
A legendary sage-emperor of high antiquity, held up by Confucius as a model ruler whose virtue was so vast the people could find no name for it.
A legendary sage-emperor, successor to Yao, likewise praised by Confucius as a model of effortless, virtuous rule.
The legendary founder-emperor Yu the Great, praised by Confucius for personal frugality, devotion to the spirits, and his labors on flood-control channels. (Not the disciples named Yu.)
King Wen of Zhou, the revered founder-figure of the Chau (Zhou) dynasty, embodiment of virtuous rule before the dynasty's full establishment.
King Wu of Zhou, son of King Wan, who completed the founding of the Chau dynasty and boasted of his ten able ministers.
The Duke of Zhou, brother of King Wu, model statesman and architect of Zhou institutions; Confucius so revered him that he measured his own decline by no longer dreaming of him.
An ancient prince praised by Confucius for the highest virtue because he thrice yielded the throne to others without seeking any credit.
An official who threatened Confucius's life; the Master expressed calm trust that Heaven, source of his virtue, would protect him from such a man.
The first of the legendary Chinese dynasties; Confucius cites its ceremonies and rulers when discussing the inheritance of ritual across the ages.
The Shang dynasty (also called Yin), which followed the Hsia; Confucius traces how each dynasty kept and altered the rites of the one before.
The Zhou dynasty, the great house under which Confucius lived (though in decline); he admired its refined institutions above all earlier ones and declared 'I follow Chau'.
An ancient piece of ceremonial music associated with the sage-king Shun; Confucius judged it 'perfectly beautiful and also perfectly good' and was entranced by it for three months.
An ancient piece of ceremonial music associated with King Wu; Confucius judged it perfectly beautiful but not perfectly good, since it celebrated conquest.
The opening ode of the Book of Poetry, praised by Confucius as expressing joy without excess and used as a model of music's right effect.
The ancient divination classic, the Book of Changes (I Ching), which Confucius wished he had more years to study so as to avoid great faults.
The Book of History (or Book of Documents), an ancient collection of speeches and records of early rulers that Confucius quotes on filial duty and government.
A conventional measure of a medium-to-large feudal state's military and wealth — a country able to field a thousand war-chariots. Confucius uses it to picture the scale of governing.
An ancient Chinese unit of distance (a few hundred meters), used here to size a small state — 'a state of a hundred li'. (Not to be confused with li meaning ritual propriety.)
A solemn imperial ancestral rite (the di sacrifice); Confucius treats its full meaning as so profound that whoever truly grasped it could govern the world with ease.
The Son of Heaven, the title of the supreme ruler (king or emperor), who alone holds Heaven's mandate to rule all under heaven.
In Legge's rendering, the ruler of a state or one's lord — the sovereign a minister serves — rather than merely a king's son.
Legge's rendering of ren, the supreme Confucian ideal: complete human goodness or benevolence toward others. The hardest virtue to attain and the heart of Confucius's teaching.
Legge's rendering of li, the proper rituals, manners, and rules of conduct that govern how a person should behave in every situation. Often phrased 'the rules of propriety.'
Tian, the highest power in Confucian thought — a moral, ordering force of the cosmos rather than a personal god. It assigns each person's fate ('the appointments of Heaven').
Confucius's principle that words must match reality: a ruler must truly be a ruler, a father truly a father, before society can function. Setting language right is the first step in good government.
A person of the highest possible wisdom and virtue, even rarer than the superior man — the legendary ideal of human perfection.
A high official (Meng Jingzi) of the state of Lu who visited the dying disciple Tsang.
The Duke of Zhou, a revered early statesman of the Zhou dynasty whom Confucius held up as a model of wisdom and good government.
The Zhou dynasty (and its ruling house), the long era Confucius idealized as a golden age of proper ritual and government.
The Yin (Shang) dynasty that the Zhou replaced. Confucius treats its late rulers as examples of misrule.
Legendary golden ages — the eras of the sage-emperors Yao (T'ang) and Shun (Yu) — invoked as times rich in talented men.
The music-master of Lu, praised by Confucius for the magnificent performance of the Kwan Tsu music.
The opening ode of the Book of Poetry, here named for its grand musical setting.
A village whose unnamed inhabitant remarked on the breadth, but lack of single fame, of Confucius's learning.
A town where Confucius was once detained and threatened; he calmly trusted that Heaven would not let his mission perish.
The fenghuang or phoenix, a mythical bird whose appearance was an omen that a sage ruler had arisen. Its absence means the age is bad.

glossary.term: the river sends forth no map
glossary.gloss: An allusion to a legendary auspicious chart said to rise from the Yellow River in a sage's reign. Its absence, like the phoenix's, means good government will not come in Confucius's time.

glossary.term: the nine wild tribes of the east
glossary.gloss: Peoples on the eastern frontier regarded as uncivilized; Confucius mused that a superior man's presence would refine even them.
aliases: nine wild tribes of the east

glossary.gloss: Evergreens used by Confucius as an image of steadfast character: like trees that keep their leaves when winter comes, the virtuous show their worth in hard times.
A disciple of Confucius, quoted briefly recalling a saying of the Master.
A ceremonial jade tablet (gui) carried by an official as a token of his ruler's authority; handling it required great care and reverence.
The hall where a family or ruling house honored its ancestors with sacrifices and ritual — a central site of Confucian ceremony.
A belt or sash worn at the waist, here part of formal dress and its ceremonial appendages.
A formal visit or expression of sympathy to the bereaved. A 'visit of condolence' called for somber, ceremonial dress.
Disease-bringing evil spirits or forces; villagers held ceremonies to drive them away, and Confucius dressed formally for the occasion.
Two states where Confucius and his followers were stranded and went hungry during their wanderings — a famous hardship recalled with affection.
Ran Boniu, a disciple of Confucius ranked among those distinguished for virtuous conduct.
Ran You (Ran Qiu), a capable disciple skilled in administration, who served the Ji family. Often called Ch'iu or simply Zan.
Another name for the disciple Tsze-lu (Zilu) when serving in office.
The outer wooden case enclosing a coffin — a mark of an elaborate, costly burial.
Nanrong, a disciple of careful character to whom Confucius gave his niece in marriage.
Gongxi Hua, a young disciple modest about his abilities who wished to serve as a minor assistant in temple ceremonies. Also called Ch'ih.
Gao Chai (Tsze-kao), a disciple whom Confucius described as 'simple' or guileless.
The personal name of the disciple Tsang (Zengzi), here described as 'dull' or slow.
The personal name of the disciple Tsze-chang, called 'specious' and one who 'goes beyond the due mean.'

glossary.term: altars of the spirits of the land and grain
glossary.gloss: The shrines to the local guardian spirits of the soil and the harvest — symbols of the welfare of a state.
The Yi River, where the disciple Tien imagined bathing on a spring outing — Confucius's favorite of the disciples' wishes.
Open-air altars used in ceremonies praying for rain; a pleasant place to take the breeze in Tien's vision.
Zeng Dian (Tsang Hsi), father of the disciple Tsang, whose modest wish for a spring outing won Confucius's approval.
The murder of a king or sovereign — a crime Confucius's disciples would never abet, even under a wicked chief.
The murder of one's own father (or close kin) — paired with regicide as the ultimate crime a loyal minister would refuse.
Sima Niu, a disciple, anxious and talkative, who questioned Confucius about virtue and about having no brothers.
The bounds of the known world; 'all within the four seas' means all people everywhere.
A recurring topic in the Analects: for Confucius, ruling well means leading by moral example and keeping each person true to their role, not by force or law.
Duke Ai of Lu, the reigning ruler of Confucius's home state, who occasionally consulted him.
Youzi (You Ruo), a disciple of Confucius, here advising Duke Ai to lighten taxes for the people's good.
To tax at one tenth. Yu Zo urges the duke to take only a tenth of the harvest rather than burdening the people more heavily.
Duke Jing of the state of Ch'i, who asked Confucius about government and received the famous answer about each person keeping to their role.
Loving concern for all people — Legge's word here for ren, the same ideal he elsewhere calls 'perfect virtue.' Confucius defines it simply as 'to love all men.'
A legendary wise minister of the sage-emperor Shun, cited as proof that promoting the upright drives out the wicked.
The virtuous founder of the Shang dynasty, who like Shun raised up worthy ministers (here, I Yin).
A famous wise minister whom T'ang promoted from obscurity, used as an example of choosing virtuous officials.
Farming; the work of cultivating crops. Confucius declined to teach it, saying a ruler need not master farming to govern well.
The Duke (governor) of She, a district of the state of Ch'u, who questioned Confucius about government and uprightness.
Duke Ding of Lu, who asked Confucius whether a single saying could make or ruin a country.
A town in Lu where the disciple Tsze-hsia served as governor.
The balanced middle course between excess and deficiency — the Confucian ideal of moderation, also called the due mean.
Excessively flattering; fawning. The mean man flatters but is not genuinely warm, whereas the superior man is warm without flattery.
Friendly and easy in manner. Confucius says the superior man is affable without sinking into flattery.
Yuan Xian (Tsze-ssu), a disciple who asked Confucius what is truly shameful. (Distinct from the official Hsien in Book XIV's later chapters.)
Greedy craving for wealth or possessions — a fault Confucius lists among those that must be repressed to approach virtue.
A legendary strongman of antiquity, said to be able to move a boat on dry land, who nonetheless died a violent death — cited as a warning that brute strength is not virtue.
Hou Ji, the legendary ancestor of the Zhou and patron of agriculture, who 'wrought at husbandry' and came to possess the kingdom.
Zichan of Zheng, a celebrated statesman of Confucius's era whom the Master praised as a kind and able man. He lived at Tung-li.
The district where the statesman Tsze-ch'an lived.
An official of Zheng who drafted the state's diplomatic documents, named in praise of the care Zheng took with its writings.
An official of Zheng who reviewed and discussed the state's draft documents.
A town of three hundred families taken from the Po family by Kwan Chung; also the home of the brave Chwang.
Meng Gongchuo, an official Confucius judged fit to advise great families but not to govern a small state. Also called Kung-ch'o.
Two powerful noble families (later states), in whose households Mang Kung-ch'o was deemed fit to serve.
Two small states; Confucius said Mang Kung-ch'o was unsuited to be a high officer in either. (Tang here = the small state Teng.)
A man of Pien famed for bravery, cited by Confucius as the model of courage in the 'complete man.'
Confucius's ideal of an all-round accomplished person — combining wisdom, freedom from greed, courage, talent, and ritual refinement.
Gongshu Wenzi, an official of Wei praised for speaking, laughing, and taking only when fitting; honored after death with the title 'Wan' (the Accomplished).
Gongming Jia, who reported to Confucius on the measured character of his master Kung-shu Wan.
A fortified town that Tsang Wu-chung held while pressing a demand on the duke of Lu.
Duke Wen of Jin, a leading lord of the era whom Confucius judged 'crafty and not upright.'
The powerful northern state of Jin, ruled by Duke Wan.
Duke Huan of Ch'i, the first great hegemon among the lords, whom Confucius judged 'upright and not crafty.' Served by Kwan Chung.
A brother of Duke Hwan whom Hwan had killed in a struggle for power; his death tested the loyalty of Kwan Chung.
A retainer of the prince Chiu who chose to die with his master, contrasted with Kwan Chung, who lived on to serve the rival.
A sign of barbarism in Confucius's eyes; he credits Kwan Chung's statesmanship with saving Chinese civilization from being overrun. 'Buttoning on the left side' is the same image.
Duke Ling of Wei, a ruler Confucius called unprincipled yet who kept his state thanks to capable officers.
Chen Heng, a minister of Ch'i who murdered his own sovereign, Duke Chien — prompting Confucius to urge a punitive expedition.
Duke Jian of Ch'i, murdered by his minister Chan Ch'ang.
The three great noble clans (the Meng, Shu, and Ji families) that effectively controlled the state of Lu, often over the duke himself.
Qu Boyu, an official of Wei admired by Confucius for constantly striving to reduce his own faults.
To repay or pay back. Confucius advises repaying injury with justice and kindness with kindness.
Gongbo Liao, a man who slandered the disciple Tsze-lu; Confucius shrugged off the threat as beyond his control, in Heaven's hands.
Zifu Jingbo, an official who warned Confucius of the slander against Tsze-lu and offered to punish the slanderer.
The head of the Ji clan of Lu, to whom Kung-po Liao spread his slander.
A gate or place where Tsze-lu lodged for a night; its gatekeeper recognized Confucius as the man who keeps trying though the times are hopeless.
A stone chime (qing), a hanging slab struck to make a clear musical note, which Confucius is described playing in Wei.
King Wu Ding (Gaozong) of the Shang dynasty, cited as an example of a sovereign observing the three-year silence of imperial mourning.
The Book of Documents (Shujing), one of the ancient classics, quoted on the mourning customs of Kao-tsung.
An old acquaintance of Confucius who sat rudely sprawling; Confucius rebuked him as a useless 'pest' and tapped his shin with a staff.
A village whose ambitious young messenger Confucius judged to be hurrying to seem grown rather than truly to learn.
The lower leg or shin — where Confucius struck the sprawling Yuan Zang with his staff.
An able officer of Wei in charge of receiving guests, one of the capable ministers who kept Duke Ling's state intact.
An officer of Wei in charge of the army, named among the capable ministers who preserved Duke Ling's misruled state.
Tao, the right path of life and government — the moral order Confucius urges people and rulers to follow. Legge often renders it as 'right principles' or 'the cause of truth.'
An older man who taunted Confucius for wandering about as a restless 'insinuating talker'; Confucius answered that he merely hated stubbornness.
Approval or praise. Used of the people's inability to praise T'ai-po's hidden virtue, and of learning done merely for others' approval.
Confucius's ideal: a person of cultivated virtue and integrity (the junzi). Contrasted throughout with the 'mean man' or 'small man'.
The petty or small-minded person, ruled by self-interest and appetite; the opposite of the 'superior man'.
Doing what is morally right and fitting in a situation (yi); the standard the superior man holds above mere gain or valor.
Confucius's single rule for life (shu): not doing to others what you would not want done to yourself.
The balanced middle course between extremes; here 'hold fast the due Mean' urges steady, measured conduct in rule.
The decrees or moral order of Heaven (tianming); the cosmic mandate the superior man reveres and must recognize.
The reigning emperor, who alone (in right order) issues ceremonies, music, and military expeditions.
A person of the highest wisdom and virtue; the rare ideal even above the 'superior man'.
Patient self-restraint; lacking it in small matters can wreck great plans.
To complain or feel discontent; good rule lays tasks on people 'without their repining'.
A person who has withdrawn from public life and society to live in seclusion.
An official court historian or record-keeper; Yu is praised as a straightforward one.
Ceremonial dances performed with the music (here the Shao) at court rituals.
A cloth band worn round the waist; Tsze-chang wrote his master's counsels on the end of his.
The crossbar harnessing horses to a carriage; one should keep good counsels in view as if fixed to it.
A clouding or darkening of the mind; each virtue pursued without learning brings its own 'beclouding'.
A lofty, large-spirited disregard for petty things; an ancient virtue that has degenerated into wild license.
A factional, one-sided loyalist; the superior man is sociable but never a partizan.
A bright pure red; Confucius hates how purple steals its luster, an image of the false displacing the genuine.
A stringed instrument; the Master plays and sings to it so the unwelcome Zu Pei will hear.
A shallow crossing place in a river; Tsze-lu is sent to ask the way across.
A common grain prepared as food; the old recluse cooks it for Tsze-lu.
Units of measure (about six feet each); the wall of Confucius's learning is 'several fathoms high'.
Small hills or mounds; others' merits are mere hillocks beside Confucius the sun and moon.
The Hsia (Xia) dynasty, earliest of the three, whose seasonal calendar Confucius recommended following.
The Hsia, Yin (Shang), and Chau (Zhou) dynasties, taken together as the model ages of good rule.
Kings Wen and Wu, the revered founders of the Chou dynasty whose doctrines lived on among men.
A large southern state; home of the 'madman' Chieh-yu who warned Confucius.
A small dependent territory within Lu, whose ruler kept the sacrifices to the eastern Mang; the Chi family planned to attack it.
The three great families of Lu descended from Duke Huan, who had seized the state's power.
Confucius's own son (Li); urged by his father to study the Odes and the rules of propriety.
A famously upright official, thrice dismissed yet refusing to serve crookedly or leave his home state.
The eccentric 'madman of Ch'u' who sang a warning to Confucius about the perils of public office.
A scheming official who maneuvered to draw Confucius into service; Confucius avoided then met him.
The ruler of Ch'i who, despite a thousand teams of horses, won no praise for any virtue at his death.
A sacred mountain (Mount Meng) whose sacrifices the ruler of Chwan-yu was appointed to oversee.
A town held by the rebel Pi Hsi, who invited Confucius to join him.
All the lands and peoples of the kingdom; T'ang takes their offenses upon himself.
The sovereign's humble self-reference, bearing the people's blame alone.
The long mourning period observed for a dead parent, defended by Confucius against shortening it.
The dignified court music of the Odes, which Confucius hates to hear corrupted by the songs of Chang.
Music of the state of Cheng that Confucius condemns as licentious and corrupting.
The five virtues of good government Confucius lists: beneficence, fitting labor, ambition without greed, dignified ease, and majesty without fierceness.
The four faults of bad rule Confucius names: cruelty, oppression, injury, and stingy officialism.
The high official in charge of justice and punishments in a state.
A man of virtue under the dying Yin dynasty who withdrew from the corrupt court.
A loyal minister of the last Yin king who remonstrated against him and was put to death.
